text:
alex: Quick question — running a few nsys captures to investigate a latency regression in KV fetch + batching path. My baseline command: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o out.nsys-rep --duration=8s --sample=none python run_inference.py`
maria: For our workloads I usually avoid sampling for kernel timelines (we need full CUDA timeline). Good to include osrt if using our custom CPU->GPU batching threads.
jin: FYI sampling can shrink file sizes dramatically but you lose exact kernel ordering. For root cause I prefer full trace for a short window.
sam: If file size is scary, you can limit capture with `--duration` or `--capture-range=nvtx` (mark start/end with NVTX ranges in code). That gives you the important section only.
alex: Good tip. We're seeing a ~3-4ms spike on long sequences. Thinking the kernel selection fallback triggers a slower matmul. How do people capture with minimal noise from other processes?
maria: Run on a reserved GPU node, kill background jobs, and use `--capture-child-processes=false` (or explicitly set) so you don't get unrelated process traces. Also `--force-overwrite` helps when iterating.
perf-bot: reminder: when you do full cuda+osrt+nvtx traces nsys reps can be >1GB for 8s on multi-stream heavy runs. Use `nsys stats out.nsys-rep` to get a quick condensed timeline.
jin: Another trick: do two captures — 1) short full-trace (3-10s) around the NVTX window, 2) long sampled run for stats (`--sample=cpu` or `--sample=thread`) to get call rates without massive file sizes.
sam: Also enable `--cuda-trace-api`? I usually rely on NVTX markers inside the runtime: `nvtxRangePush/Pop` around the batching and KV paths so the timeline shows the sections.
alex: Example NVTX usage in Python: ```python
import nvtx
with nvtx.annotate("kv_fetch", color="0xFF0000"):
    fetch_kv()
```
maria: When you look at the timeline, check OSRT threads for scheduling stalls. If OSRT shows big gaps and then big kernel launches, that points to batching heuristics starving the GPU until a threshold.
jin: For kernel selection issues add `env` dump to NVTX like: `nvtxRangePushA(f"model={model_name};quant={quant};seq={seq_len}")` so you can correlate which model/quant path triggered which kernels.
alex: Share after I run — I'll try a 6s full-trace with NVTX-range start/end and a 60s sampled run. Any preferred flags for reducing nsys overhead?
maria: `--sample=none` + `--trace=cuda,osrt,nvtx` is high fidelity. To reduce overhead avoid `--trace=nvtx` only if NVTX usage is low, but we rely on NVTX heavily. Also `--timeline` view in UI helps; the CLI `nsys stats` is noisy but useful.
sam: If you suspect kernel-level contention, convert the rep to a `sqlite` and run `nsys stats -r kernel out.nsys-rep -o kernel.csv` then grep hotspots. Works well with our perf scripts.
perf-bot: pro tip: compress the .nsys-rep with `nsys export -f sqlite -o out.db out.nsys-rep` to extract smaller artifacts.
alex: Running now, will paste the rep link and a tiny summary. Thanks for the tips — NVTX ranges + short full-trace + long sampled seems like a good combo.
maria: One more — capture a control run with quantized model variant that uses the fast kernel path; compare kernel names and durations to see if fallback was used.
jin: Also check for unexpected memcpy patterns — small fragmented memcpy can indicate KV copying inefficiency. NVTX around the KV marshalling helps there too.
alex: Got it. Will post results in this thread when it's up. Thanks!
